title: Find and reset a tripped breaker safely
mechanism_check: A tripped breaker sits between ON and OFF; the trip is protection working, not a malfunction.
Breakers trip from overload (too much load) or fault (short/ground) — resetting without finding the cause invites a repeat.
Know the panel directory: which breaker feeds the dead area.
improvised_tools: A flashlight; dry hands and dry floor.
The panel directory — make one now if it doesn't exist.
steps: Unplug or switch off loads on the dead circuit first.
Find the breaker resting between ON and OFF; push it fully OFF, then firmly ON.
If it holds, add loads back one at a time to find the culprit.
If it trips instantly with nothing plugged in: that's a fault — leave it OFF and call an electrician.
stop_conditions: Burning smell, scorch marks, buzzing, or heat at the panel: stop — do not reset; call an electrician.
Breaker trips instantly on reset with no load: fault territory, not DIY.

title: Confirm a circuit is dead before touching anything
mechanism_check: Breakers can be mislabeled; one box can hold two circuits; switches can be wired to interrupt the neutral.
Trust only a test you perform yourself, on the exact wires you'll touch.
Test the tester: verify your lamp/tester works on a known-live outlet first.
improvised_tools: A plug-in lamp or radio as a tester (it either runs or it doesn't).
A non-contact voltage tester if you have one — still back it with the lamp test.
steps: Plug the lamp into the outlet/fixture and confirm it lights.
Switch off the breaker you believe feeds it; confirm the lamp dies.
Test the lamp on a known-live outlet to prove the lamp still works.
Only then touch the wiring — and treat it as live anyway while working.
stop_conditions: Lamp stays lit after the breaker is off: wrong breaker — stop and map the panel properly.
Any sparking, crackling, or warmth in the box: stop and call an electrician.

title: Replace a switch or outlet cover plate safely
mechanism_check: The cover plate is cosmetic; the device and wiring behind it are live.
Cracked plates expose live terminals — replacement is safety, not vanity.
improvised_tools: A flathead screwdriver; the new plate.
Dry hands; good light so you can see what you're doing.
steps: You may leave the breaker on for a plate-only swap — but test-dead is always safer.
Remove the single center screw and lift the old plate straight off.
Fit the new plate without touching the device or wires behind it.
Tighten gently — overtightening cracks the new plate.
stop_conditions: Wires or device visibly damaged behind the plate: stop — that's device replacement, call an electrician.
Plate won't sit flat because the box is recessed: use a box extender, not force.

title: Triage a lamp that won't turn on
mechanism_check: Work the chain: bulb -> socket -> switch -> cord -> plug -> outlet.
A bulb that works elsewhere proves the lamp is the problem; a lamp that works elsewhere proves the outlet is.
improvised_tools: A known-good bulb for swap-testing; eyes for cord damage.
A different outlet to isolate outlet vs lamp.
steps: Swap in a known-good bulb.
Try the lamp in a known-good outlet.
Inspect the cord for nicks, kinks, and heat damage; check the plug prongs.
Look inside the socket for a flattened center tab — unplug first, then lift it slightly with a wooden stick.
stop_conditions: Cord damaged, melted, or hot: stop using the lamp — replace the cord or the lamp.
Socket scorched or loose in the housing: the lamp needs rewiring or replacing.

title: Find what's overloading a circuit
mechanism_check: Circuits are rated in amps (usually 15 or 20); loads add up in watts / volts = amps.
Heating appliances (space heaters, hair dryers, microwaves) are the usual hogs at 1200-1800W each.
A breaker at 80%+ of rating for sustained periods will eventually trip.
improvised_tools: Paper and pencil: list every device on the circuit with its wattage (on the label).
The panel directory to map which outlets share the circuit.
steps: Map the circuit: switch the breaker off and see what dies.
List every load with its watts; divide by 120 for amps.
Move the biggest hog to a different circuit.
If the total is legitimately under rating and it still trips: that's a fault — electrician.
stop_conditions: Tempted to swap in a bigger breaker: stop — the breaker protects the wire; a bigger breaker lets the wire overheat.
Warm outlets or a warm breaker: stop and call an electrician — heat means resistance means fault.

title: Retire a damaged extension cord safely
mechanism_check: Cut insulation, exposed conductors, loose prongs, and melted spots are all retirement criteria — not repair criteria.
A damaged cord is a shock and fire source; tape over damage is not a fix.
improvised_tools: Wire cutters or scissors to destroy the cord so nobody fishes it out of the trash.
A replacement cord rated for the load (gauge and length matter).
steps: Unplug the cord.
Cut the cord into short pieces — especially the plug end — so it can't be reused.
Dispose of the pieces.
Replace with a cord rated for the actual load and length.
stop_conditions: Cord is hardwired into equipment: stop — that's a repair job, not a retirement.
Damage from a fault that also damaged the outlet: check the outlet before plugging anything new in.
